title: What's this? Whose is it?
title_target: นี่อะไร ของใคร — Nîi à-rai, khǎawng khrai
goal: Point at things, ask "what's this", say what there is and isn't, and say whose something is — four short patterns used dozens of times a day.

ask นี่อะไร and answer it

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — At the desk, Monday morning
dialogs.intro: Nok finds things left behind in the meeting room. Notice the difference between demonstratives that stand alone and those attached to a noun — in writing just one mark is different, but the tone changes.

lines.speaker: บูดี:
lines.text: [มี|Mii][ครับ|khráp] [นี่|Nîi][ครับ|khráp]

notes: **Thai demonstratives come in pairs, and the pairs differ by TONE.** The ones that **stand alone** have a falling tone: *นี่ nîi, นั่น nân, โน่น nôon*. The ones **attached to a noun** have a high tone: *นี้ níi, นั้น nán, โน้น nóon*. Compare: *นี่กระเป๋า* (this is a bag) with *กระเป๋าใบนี้* (this bag).

**There are THREE distances, not two.** *นี่* = near the speaker (this). *นั่น* = near the listener (that). *โน่น* = far from both (that over there). English uses "that" for the last two; Thai separates them, rather like the old English "yonder".
**The classifier is required in the pointing pattern.** "This bag" is *กระเป๋า**ใบ**นี้*, not *กระเป๋านี้*. This follows straight on from Unit 4, and it's where beginners forget most often.

**มี mii means both "there is" and "to have"** — one word for both. *ผมมีรถ* (I have a car), *ที่นี่มีร้านกาแฟ* (there's a coffee shop here). The negative is *ไม่มี mâi mii*, a phrase you'll hear and say very often.
**ของ khǎawng means "belonging to", and it comes before the owner.** *ของผม* (mine), *ของนก* (Nok's), *ของใคร* (whose). In fast speech *ของ* is often **dropped**: *กระเป๋าผม* is enough for "my bag".
**เอง eeng means "self" and adds emphasis.** *ของผมเอง* = "my own". It's also used for "I did it myself": *ทำเอง tham eeng* (make it yourself).

**ไม่ใช่ mâi châi means "is not", and it's DIFFERENT from ไม่ mâi.** *ไม่ใช่* negates **a noun or an identity**: *ไม่ใช่ของผม* (it's not mine). *ไม่* negates **a verb or an adjective**: *ไม่ชอบ* (don't like), *ไม่แพง* (not expensive). ⚠️ Swapping them is the mistake a Thai ear catches fastest.
**เดี๋ยว dǐao means "in a moment", and it signals immediate intent.** *เดี๋ยวถามเขา* = "I'll ask him in a bit". Said on its own, *เดี๋ยวๆ dǐao-dǐao* means "wait, wait".

rows: ที่โน่น *thîi-nôon* — over there

after: Two very common derivatives: **แบบนี้ *bàaep-níi*** (like this) and **อย่างนั้น *yàang-nán*** (like that). Both turn up in conversation every day.

grammars.title: มี, ไม่มี, and how to ask
body: These rows cover almost every "there is / there isn't" need at A1.

head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: มีร้านกาแฟ
มีปากกาไหม
ที่นี่มีห้องน้ำ
มี + noun + กี่ + classifier
มีพี่น้องกี่คน
how many siblings do you have?

after: ⚠️ The short answer to a *มี…ไหม* question isn't "yes/no" but **repeating the verb**: *มีครับ* (I do / there is) or *ไม่มีครับ* (I don't / there isn't). Thai answers questions by repeating the verb — this pattern works for almost every question and will come back in every unit that follows.

grammars.title: Ownership: ของ and how to use it

head: Thai
Pronunciation
Meaning
rows: ของผม / ของฉัน
ไม่ใช่ของผม

after: *ของ* also means "things, stuff" when it stands alone: *ซื้อของ súue khǎawng* = to go shopping (literally "buy things"). The word returns in Unit 14.

sections.title: Prepositions of place: the six most common

head: Thai
Pronunciation
Meaning
Example
rows: บนโต๊ะ — on the table
ใต้เก้าอี้ — under the chair
ในกระเป๋า — in the bag
หน้า / หลัง
หน้าร้าน — in front of the shop

blocks.text: The word *ข้าง khâang* is often attached in front of the others to form place nouns: *ข้างใน khâang-nai* (inside), *ข้างนอก khâang-nâwk* (outside), *ข้างบน khâang-bon* (above, upstairs), *ข้างล่าง khâang-lâang* (below, downstairs). These four words turn up in every building you enter.

blocks.title: Finding something you've lost
items: **หาไม่เจอ *hǎa mâi joee*** — I can't find it. The most useful sentence when you're panicking.
**เห็น…ไหม *hěn … mǎi*** — have you seen …? *เห็นกุญแจผมไหมครับ* = have you seen my keys?
**อยู่ตรงนี้ *yùu trong-níi*** — it's right here. The word *ตรง trong* means "right at", and adding it makes pointing more precise: *ตรงนั้น* = right there.
